Likelihood of local presences under the DAMOCLES model

Source: R/damocles.R
damocles_loglik.Rd

damocles_loglik() computes the exact log-likelihood of the presences and absences of the species of a clade in a local community, given their tree and the rates of local colonisation gamma and extinction mu, under the model of simulate_damocles(). It follows the pruning algorithm of Pigot & Etienne (2015, Box 1): from the tips to the root, the probabilities of the observed states below each branch, given its state, are carried along the branch by the analytical solution of the backward equations of the two-state process, and combined at each node by the rule of speciation (allopatric, or with probability sympatry leaving both daughters present). fit_damocles() finds the maximum-likelihood rates, and optionally sympatry.

Usage

damocles_loglik(
  comm,
  tree,
  gamma,
  mu,
  root = c("both", "absent", "present"),
  sympatry = 0
)

fit_damocles(
  comm,
  tree,
  root = c("both", "absent", "present"),
  start = NULL,
  shared = FALSE,
  sympatry = 0,
  regimes = NULL,
  edge_covariate = NULL,
  vary = c("both", "gamma", "mu")
)

Arguments

comm

Presences of the species (columns, named as the tips of tree) in one or more communities (rows): a matrix or data frame, or a named vector for one community. Values above zero count as presences. Tips missing from comm count as absent, with a warning, and species of comm missing from the tree are dropped.

tree

A rooted, fully dichotomous phylo tree with branch lengths.

gamma

Rate of local colonisation per lineage, in the units of the branch lengths: one rate, or one per edge of tree in the order of tree$edge.

mu

Rate of local extinction per lineage, one or one per edge. With rates per edge and a root edge, the two edges leaving the root must have the same rates, which the root edge takes.

root

Prior on the state of the ancestor at the root: "both", "absent" or "present".

sympatry

In damocles_loglik(), the probability that a present ancestor leaves both daughters present (see simulate_damocles()). In fit_damocles(), a fixed value, or NULL to estimate it with the rates (shared or not, as they are).

start

Optional starting rates, c(gamma = , mu = ); by default the optimisation starts from four combinations of 0.2 and 2 divided by the height of the tree.

shared

If TRUE, one set of parameters shared by all communities, estimated from the sum of their log-likelihoods; if FALSE (the default), separate parameters for each community.

regimes

Optional regime of each edge of tree, in the order of tree$edge (a factor or character vector), such as from clade_regimes() or from a configuration of rate shifts estimated by another method: the rates in vary are estimated separately for each regime.

edge_covariate

Optional positive number for each edge of tree, in the order of tree$edge, such as branch-specific rates of speciation estimated by another method: the rates in vary change with it as \(\mathrm{rate} \cdot (x / \bar{x}_g)^\beta\), where \(x\) is the covariate and \(\bar{x}_g\) its geometric mean, with rate and \(\beta\) estimated. Give regimes or edge_covariate, not both.

vary

Which rates change among regimes or with edge_covariate: "both", "gamma" or "mu"; the other one is a single rate for the whole tree.

Value

damocles_loglik(): the log-likelihood of each community. fit_damocles(): a data frame of class mc_damocles_fit with one row per community and the columns gamma, mu, sympatry (fixed or estimated), loglik, richness and convergence (0 when stats::optim() converged). With shared = TRUE every row holds the same rates and convergence code, loglik is the contribution of each community at those rates, and the attribute loglik_total holds their sum.

Details

At the root, "both" averages the likelihoods given an absent and a present ancestor, as the default of the DAMOCLES package (pchoice = 0); the article sums them, which only adds log(2) to the log-likelihood. The optimisation works on the logarithm of the rates, with stats::optim() from several starting points, so estimates of zero appear as very small rates. Under this model the tip states hold information on gamma and mu only through their pattern on the tree, so with few species, or with a community holding nearly all or nearly none of them, the likelihood surface is flat and the estimates are poor. In data-raw/validation_damocles.R, ten communities simulated with gamma = mu = 1 on trees of 60 tips gave estimates of mu from zero to several thousand, with the same likelihoods as DAMOCLES::DAMOCLES_ML(); the ratio of the two rates is better estimated than each one.

With shared = TRUE, fit_damocles() estimates one pair of rates for all communities by maximising the sum of their log-likelihoods, which treats the communities as independent realisations of the same process on the same tree. Pooling communities narrows the estimates: in data-raw/validation_damocles.R, with gamma = mu = 1 on trees of 60 tips and height one (30 fits each), 90% of the estimates of gamma fell between 0.49 and 6.0 from one community and between 0.75 and 1.27 from twenty, and those of mu between zero and 18.9 from one and between zero and 1.8 from twenty. mu stays the harder rate, and some fits still put it near zero. The assumption of independence matters: neighbouring sites that share their colonisation history, or communities nested in one another, are not independent replicates and pooling them overstates the information on the rates. Twice the difference between the summed log-likelihoods of separate and shared fits can be compared with a chi-squared distribution on \(2 (m - 1)\) degrees of freedom, with \(m\) communities, to ask whether the rates differ among communities.

With sympatry = NULL, fit_damocles() also estimates the probability that a present ancestor leaves both daughters present, on the logit scale. A single community says almost nothing about it: in data-raw/validation_damocles.R, with sympatry = 0.5 and gamma = mu = 1 on trees of 60 tips, 90% of the estimates fell between 0 and 1 from one community, between 0.26 and 0.81 from five and between 0.41 and 0.60 from twenty. Estimate it with shared rates, and compare the fit with that of sympatry = 0 by a likelihood ratio (one degree of freedom, on the boundary of the parameter space, so the chi-squared p-value is conservative) to ask whether strictly allopatric speciation is enough.

Rates can change across the tree. damocles_loglik() and simulate_damocles() take one rate per edge, and fit_damocles() estimates rates that differ among regimes of the edges (a partition defined a priori with clade_regimes(), or the configuration of rate shifts of a method such as BAMM) or that change with an edge_covariate (such as branch-specific rates of speciation from a method such as ClaDS), for colonisation, extinction or both (vary). Either input is a plain vector in the order of tree$edge, so any method can supply it. Rates of diversification describe speciation and extinction of the whole lineage, not local colonisation and extinction: the regimes or the covariate are a hypothesis about the local dynamics, tested by comparing the fit with the constant model by damocles_lrt() (a single regime, or beta = 0, gives the constant model) and by intervals from confint.mc_damocles_fit(). Each regime adds parameters to a likelihood that is already flat, so these fits need several communities with shared = TRUE; the type I error and power of that comparison are in data-raw/validation_damocles.R: with rates shared by 5 or 20 communities on trees of 60 tips, the test rejected constant rates in 4–7% of 100 replicates without an effect and in 86–99% with a threefold difference between clades or a slope of one on an autocorrelated covariate. Those communities were simulated independently; real communities that share their history will reject more often.

References

Pigot, A. L., & Etienne, R. S. (2015). A new dynamic null model for phylogenetic community structure. Ecology Letters, 18, 153–163. doi:10.1111/ele.12395

See also

simulate_damocles(), damocles_test().

Examples

set.seed(2)
tr <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(60)
comm <- simulate_damocles(tr, gamma = 1, mu = 2, n = 2)
damocles_loglik(comm, tr, gamma = 1, mu = 2)
#>      sim1      sim2 
#> -28.13747 -22.54596 
fit_damocles(comm, tr)
#> DAMOCLES rates by maximum likelihood (Pigot & Etienne 2015)
#>      gamma       mu sympatry loglik richness convergence
#> sim1 1.794 4.61e+00        0  -27.8       11           0
#> sim2 0.476 1.46e-09        0  -21.9        8           0
fit_damocles(comm, tr, shared = TRUE)
#> DAMOCLES rates by maximum likelihood (Pigot & Etienne 2015)
#> Parameters shared by 2 communities; total log-likelihood -50.6593 
#>      gamma   mu sympatry loglik richness convergence
#> sim1  1.12 2.69        0  -28.0       11           0
#> sim2  1.12 2.69        0  -22.6        8           0
